claims.text: The target nanoparticles contain five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and begin as a room-temperature single-phase solid solution.
Larger grains and lower defect densities impede atomic diffusion pathways.
Impeded atomic diffusion kinetically suppresses high-temperature elemental migration.
Elemental migration can lead to phase separation or compositional segregation.
Finer grains or higher defect densities accelerate diffusion.
Accelerated diffusion in fine-grained or highly defective nanoparticles causes instability during catalytic and thermoelectric operation.
Grain boundaries and defect sites are preferential pathways for atomic diffusion and segregation.
Larger grains and fewer defects increase the kinetic barrier to atomic diffusion.
Delaying elemental migration helps preserve a single-phase state.
Fine-grained nanoparticles provide more diffusion-active sites, accelerating thermally activated segregation and possible phase separation.
Under identical operation, the larger-grained nanoparticles will retain the initial single-phase structure with less surface segregation than the finer-grained nanoparticles.
The finer-grained nanoparticles will exhibit phase separation, elemental segregation, or clustering relative to the initial homogeneous baseline.
The proposed grain-size and defect-density mechanism should remain the dominant stability mechanism for high-entropy nanoparticles under steady operation without additional external stresses.
Changing the particular metal mixture may quantitatively change diffusion rates.
Oxidation or secondary reactions in reactive environments may influence nanoparticle stability.
Controlled annealing will produce the larger-grained comparison set, while rapid quenching will produce the finer-grained set.

contradictions.description: The intervention says grain size and defect density are controlled, but the proposed sets intentionally vary both together: large grain/low defect versus fine grain/high defect. This covariation prevents distinguishing which variable governs any observed effect.
The boundary limits the prediction to steady operating conditions, whereas the falsification experiment uses temperature cycling from 473 K to 1923 K, which is not a steady thermal condition.
